courseEvidencePolicy: Current workbook profile/topics/methods alongside official attributes where available; description2 given full consideration when enrichment is absent. No Excel edits or enrichment regeneration.
screening: All 151 current course identities screened; read the content of all plausible myth, philosophy, art, archaeology, literature, media, sociology, history, law, psychology, conflict and methods candidates. No hidden religion course is inferred from a title or free project choice. The misinformation course’s myth-debunking is a different meaning of myth; 2Spirit in Native American history does not itself establish religious studies. Code/name screening and keyword hits were leads only; substantive judgments follow actual course evidence.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.finding: Academic writing, research literacy, collaboration and reflective civic inquiry; mandatory Year-1 course.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.finding: Legal traditions and public/private law introduce institutions, rights and socio-legal inquiry. No religion-focused research sequence is documented.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.finding: Modernity, ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration and decolonisation supply historical explanation of social change. Religious history is not its sustained documented object.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.finding: Compares imperial authority, ideology, legitimacy, culture and legacies through sources and an essay. Relevant to religion/power questions but not a continuing religious-history sequence.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.finding: Indigenous history, colonial institutions, cultural resurgence, storytelling and community collaboration address lived identities and knowledge. Religion-specific inquiry cannot be inferred merely from Indigenous or 2Spirit identity.

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.finding: Freedom of religion is explicitly taught within human-rights law and philosophy, alongside dignity, universality and other rights.

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.finding: Legal sources, self-determination, human rights, force and treaty politics support institutional and conflict analysis, rather than a religion-and-politics sequence.

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.finding: The official description explicitly includes religious constitutions; comparative rights, institutions and case analysis provide a real public-religion connection. Do not expand this topic into sustained religious-studies teaching.

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.finding: EU institutions, citizenship, free movement and judicial casework provide tools for public institutions and rights questions. Religious communities or pluralism are not specified as its organising subject.

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.finding: Arguments about God, meaning and Buddhist non-self occur within a broad ancient-to-contemporary philosophical introduction.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.finding: Divine command, moral universality, Nietzsche, goodness, death and meaning connect to belief and values; most of the course develops general ethical reasoning.

GOSPHIL214.name: Philosophy of Mind
GOSPHIL214.finding: Buddhist accounts of non-self contribute to philosophical selfhood alongside neuropsychology, physicalism, AI and experience. This is a genuine connection, not a general Buddhism survey.

GOSPHIL311.name: Philosophy of Emotion
GOSPHIL311.finding: Greek and Indian accounts, love, fear, grief, moral and political emotions develop phenomenological and argumentative inquiry. Religious experience is not established as a continuing focus.

GOSPHIL313.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
GOSPHIL313.finding: Greek and Indian agency, foreknowledge, fatalism, responsibility and time support worldview questions. The course is not documented as teaching contemporary spirituality or religious traditions.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.finding: Original political texts develop authority, rights, human nature and ideology in historical context. Religious political thought is not an independent taught sequence in this evidence.

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.finding: Democracy, institutions, participation, polarisation and empirical research support public-life inquiry; the documentation does not specify religion as a sustained explanatory object.

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.finding: IR theories, geopolitical cases and a Security Council simulation analyse conflict and institutions. Religion-specific content cannot be supplied by choosing a possible case.

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.finding: Globalisation and policy analysis use a sugar case and policy memos; these are specific policy methods, not evidence of religious-policy teaching.

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.finding: Reconciliation, arts and religion are explicit topics within interdisciplinary conflict, peacebuilding and justice. This connection matters but does not turn the whole social trial into sustained religion research.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.finding: Classical theory, solidarity, identity, othering and inequality develop analysis of social life. The selected content does not document a sociology-of-religion sequence.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.finding: Interviews, ethnography, participant observation, coding and qualitative research projects support the target’s fieldwork methods. A religious community focus is not a specified taught requirement.

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.finding: Modernity, phenomenology, interactionism, Bourdieu, coloniality and theory-guided empirical interpretation support culture and identity analysis; no religious-studies subject sequence follows automatically.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.finding: Trust, solidarity, public spheres, social movements and civil repair support research on collective institutions. A freely chosen religious organisation cannot establish a taught religion focus.

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.finding: Social cognition, self, influence, persuasion, groups and prejudice provide theories of human social behaviour. A proposed study is not an empirical investigation of religious belief or practice.

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.finding: Radicalisation, belonging, dialogue, media literacy and educational toolkits support conflict and identity interests. Religious extremism is not the whole course and no religious-tradition expertise is inferred.

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.finding: Western painting is related to religious as well as social/political change, with close visual analysis and a painting research paper.

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.finding: Ancient objects and craft communities are interpreted in relation to religion, status, gender, exchange and environment. Catalogue, drawing and craft inquiry provide real material-culture methods.

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.finding: Western African masks, sculpture and visual traditions are studied through cultural, religious and social meanings. Modernist influence, colonial collecting and restitution form further substantial strands.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.finding: The official description supports Renaissance painting, sculpture and architecture and exchanges involving Islamic Mediterranean courts, trade and colonisation. This receives full consideration without inventing detailed doctrines, assessments or a religious-art specialisation.

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.finding: The official description studies early-democratic Greece through community and material culture. It supports ancient social interpretation; ritual or doctrine is not added beyond what that description states.

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.role: Direct religion, myth and ritual connection
MCCHEAM315.finding: Athenian democracy is studied through primary texts, archaeology, art, religion, myth and ritual, with assembly simulation and research. Religious practice is an integral dimension, not dismissed as absent.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.finding: The official description supports art historiography, influential authors, aesthetics, interpretation, identity and the discipline’s global challenges. These are useful methods without proving religious subject matter.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.finding: Close reading of narrative, poetry, symbolism, allegory and drama provides concrete literary methods. These do not alone establish sacred-text traditions or religious authority.

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.finding: Ancient epic, tragedy and confessional writing support comparative interpretation of mortality, community and cultural meaning. The current evidence is not the old blanket claim that this is organised-religion teaching.

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.finding: Cross-cultural creation and divine narratives, transmission, gender, power and cultural meaning provide the strongest textual bridge. Myth theories, primary materials and research support substantial comparison; no dismissal as merely incidental.

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.finding: Life writing includes spiritual self-fashioning alongside memory, identity, embodiment, trauma and migration. Its interpretive methods support lived meanings but do not constitute empirical lived-religion training.

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.finding: Adaptation theory and close comparative literary/film analysis support relations among narrative, image and medium. The documented research is not necessarily about sacred narratives or religious reception.

MCCLITR312.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
MCCLITR312.finding: The official description supports humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic interpretations and a research project. Sacred hermeneutics is not inferred from these general methods.

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.finding: Film form, history, feminist/postcolonial interpretation and an independent project provide explicit media-analysis methods; no religious-media sequence is specified.

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.finding: Print, projection, sound and digital infrastructures link material properties to knowledge and memory. Religious text transmission is a possible application rather than established course subject matter.

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.finding: American media, social identity, Indigenous self-representation and disability-centred speculative futures support cultural-change analysis. Religious utopias or fandom-as-religion are not inferred.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.finding: Race, power, representation, observation, archival research and documentary podcast/PhotoVoice develop cultural and empirical inquiry. Religion cannot be presumed from Indigenous representation.

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.finding: Documentary history, ethnography, interviews and film production support evidence and representational ethics. This does not establish ongoing research into religious practice.

candidateAssessment.concept: Comparative religious meaning through texts, images and material culture
candidateAssessment.assessment: The closest trial combines comparative myth, literary reading, art, archaeology, religion and ritual in ancient democracy, philosophy and qualitative inquiry. Myth and religious visual or material meaning are substantive bridges. Additional literary, art-historical and social methods broaden the composition, but their documented teaching does not sustain the target’s investigation of religious traditions, sacred interpretation and lived religious practice. This is a coherent humanities composition whose object becomes wider cultural meaning, rather than a defensible whole-programme response to Religious Studies.

candidateAssessment.concept: Religion in society, identity, public life and conflict
candidateAssessment.assessment: The second trial tests social theory and qualitative research with rights, political authority, comparative institutions, conflict, social psychology and extremism prevention. Freedom of religion, religious constitutions and religion in reconciliation are real taught connections, and documentary and Indigenous history supply further forms of situated inquiry. The general courses do not document a continuing investigation of religious institutions, secularisation, religious pluralism or religious communities. Selecting a religious project topic cannot supply taught subject matter or supervision that the evidence does not establish.

candidateAssessment.concept: Lived religion, spirituality and cultural change
candidateAssessment.assessment: The third trial tests philosophical selfhood, ethics and emotion together with myth, life narrative, art, media and documentary. Buddhist non-self, spiritual self-fashioning, religious visual meaning and ancient ritual are specific relevant contributions. The wider philosophy and media sequence studies general agency, representation and culture; it does not establish sustained contemporary spirituality, Western esotericism or the empirical study of lived religion. General coherence does not repair that target-level shortfall.

sequenceReview: Foundations precede the advanced philosophical, literary, sociological, art and media work where present. The social trial follows comparative-political foundations with policy analysis and social psychology with extremism prevention. Formal prerequisite chains are earlier semesters. All 24-course trials use only covered Fall-2026-start terms. The first social selection exceeded fall capacity; replacing EU Politics with the more pertinent ethnographic/documentary method course repaired that trial without restoring offerings or changing the concept.
distinctnessAndStopping: The first trial is the closest synthesis of the strongest substantive religion-related teaching, rather than the narrow old comparative-religion palette. Social-public inquiry and lived/spiritual cultural inquiry test the other coherent generator groups sequentially. They change academic priorities and actual course sets. No alternatives are accepted, so no approved pairwise floor is claimed from these trial differences. Reject all three on target comparability, not timetable feasibility. Do not extend arbitrary generic substitutions to fill a quota. There is no requirement that 23 courses each teach religion and no disciplinary-equivalence test.
finalReason: UCR offers substantial related study in comparative myth, religious art and material culture, ancient ritual, philosophy, social inquiry and religious freedom. These connections do not develop into sustained study of religious traditions, sacred interpretation or contemporary religious practice across a full programme. The wider course combinations shift towards general cultural, philosophical or social study.
